chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'There is no oath for a son against his father, nor for an owned slave against his master, nor for a woman against her husband, nor is there a vow in disobedience, nor an oath regarding the severing of family ties.'

key_terms.قَطِيعَة الرَّحِم: Severing of family ties — one of the gravest social sins in Islamic ethics, here used to void any oath made to facilitate it
key_terms.مَعْصِيَة: Disobedience/sin — an act that violates divine command, which cannot be the object of a valid oath
key_terms.نَذْر: Vow — a conditional or unconditional promise made to God, binding under Islamic law
key_terms.يَمِين: Oath, swearing by God's name — a binding legal commitment in Islamic law (fiqh)

ai.seo_question: When is an oath (yamin) invalid in Islamic law according to the Prophet?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) transmits a ruling from the Prophet (SAWW) establishing five circumstances in which an oath or vow has no legal validity. The ruling reflects the jurisprudential principle that authority relationships — between child and parent, slave and master, wife and husband — take precedence over unilateral oath-taking. Additionally, an oath to commit a sin (ma'siya) or sever family ties (qati'at al-rahim) is invalid because no oath can legally bind a person to what God has forbidden.
